articles.excerpt: OpenAI has announced changes to how ChatGPT and Codex usage works, according to BleepingComputer. The reporting is brief, so this article covers only what is confirmed and points out what is still unk…
articles.body: OpenAI has announced changes to how ChatGPT and Codex usage works, according to BleepingComputer. The reporting is brief, so this article covers only what is confirmed and points out what is still unknown. What happened BleepingComputer reports that OpenAI has confirmed three changes: Usage limits for the Pro plan are being doubled. ChatGPT Work capabilities are being rolled out directly into regular Chat. Usage allowances across ChatGPT and Codex are being combined. The sources do not say which plans beyond Pro are affected, what the old and new limits are in concrete numbers, how the combined allowance is calculated, or when the rollout reaches all users. Those details should come from OpenAI's own announcement.
articles.author: Jathurshan Sownthararasa

articles.title: Rotifer v0.9.4: Agents get a memory of their own (npm 0.33.0)
articles.excerpt: Until now, a gene started every run from nothing. Whatever it learned about a user, a task or a recurring input was gone when the run ended. v0.9.4 gives every agent a memory. Its genes can read and w…
articles.body: Until now, a gene started every run from nothing. Whatever it learned about a user, a task or a recurring input was gone when the run ended. v0.9.4 gives every agent a memory. Its genes can read and write it between runs, through four calls, under rules the protocol defines: what kind of entry it is, who may read it, how much room there is, and how long it is kept. v0.9.4 is the protocol version (spec §38, Agent Memory). It shipped in @rotifer/playground 0.33.0 on 2026-11-01. Memory belongs to the agent, not to a gene An agent is a set of genes. Genes get replaced: a better formatter comes along, a gene gets a new version. If memory lived inside a gene, every swap would wipe what the agent had learned. So memory belongs to the agent.

articles.title: I Wanted a Workout Tracker That Respected My Data, So I Built KOVA
articles.excerpt: Building an offline-first fitness application focused on privacy, personal training history, and putting users in control of their own data. Fitness applications have an interesting business model. Yo…
articles.body: Building an offline-first fitness application focused on privacy, personal training history, and putting users in control of their own data. Fitness applications have an interesting business model. You track your workouts, record your progress, build routines, and gradually accumulate months or even years of personal training data. But where does all that information actually live? For many applications, your training history depends on an account, a cloud service, or a subscription. I started thinking about a different approach. What if a workout tracker could be genuinely useful without requiring users to depend on a remote service? That idea became KOVA . Explore KOVA Your training history should belong to you A workout tracker should be relatively simple in principle.

articles.title: I Built an Android AI Assistant That Doesn't Need the Cloud
articles.excerpt: Running language models locally on Android, keeping conversations on-device, and exploring what happens when AI doesn't depend on a server. Most AI applications have something in common. You type a me…
articles.body: Running language models locally on Android, keeping conversations on-device, and exploring what happens when AI doesn't depend on a server. Most AI applications have something in common. You type a message, send it somewhere, wait for a server to process it, and receive a response. It's convenient. It's also an architecture we've become so accustomed to that we rarely question it. What if the model didn't need to run on someone else's infrastructure? What if your phone could handle the inference itself? That question is what led me to build Snor , an Android application designed around local AI inference. Explore Snor The idea: AI without the usual cloud dependency I wanted to experiment with something different from the typical AI chatbot architecture.

articles.title: Building a Reliable Media Processing Pipeline with REST APIs
articles.excerpt: A media processing workflow can look simple at first: upload a file, send a request, and download the result. The complexity starts when the workflow needs to handle large files, network interruptions…
articles.body: A media processing workflow can look simple at first: upload a file, send a request, and download the result. The complexity starts when the workflow needs to handle large files, network interruptions, and multiple processing tasks. In this article, I will focus on a few engineering decisions that make a media pipeline more reliable. Start with Input Validation Before sending a request to a processing service, validate the input. At a minimum, check: Whether the file format is supported Whether the file size is within the allowed limit Whether the required parameters are present Whether the source file can be accessed Rejecting invalid input early is usually easier than debugging a failed processing job later.

articles.title: This Android gaming benchmark app does something I’ve never seen before
articles.excerpt: Evolve is a new gaming benchmark that shows you where mobile GPUs are hitting a bottleneck.
articles.body: Credit: Harish Jonnalagadda / Android Authority I like benchmarks a little too much and use them on every new phone I test. Synthetic benchmarks like Geekbench and 3DMark do a good job of simulating real-world usage and gaming scenarios, and they predict a device’s performance potential reasonably well. As someone who gets over 75 phones a year, a synthetic benchmark lets me easily measure how a particular device holds up against its predecessor. There’s a new benchmark that aims to go beyond just delivering an overall score. It’s called Evolve , and it provides useful insights across five metrics, allowing you to then pinpoint which part of the GPU is handling modern workloads well, and what’s causing a potential bottleneck.

articles.excerpt: From a close encounter between Mars and Jupiter to dazzling Venus and elusive Mercury, November offers plenty of planetary highlights. Here's when and where to look.
articles.body: This is a great month for planet watching, either in the evenings or mornings. During convenient evening hours, the planet of choice is Saturn , visible well up in the southern sky during mid-to-late evening hours. Telescopically, the southern side of its famous ring system is currently tilted about 6½ degrees to our line of sight. Around the middle of the night, Mars and Jupiter come into view above the east-northeast horizon and just before the break of dawn are in excellent position, soaring high in the southern sky in the vicinity of the Sickle of Leo the Lion. Watch how Mars approaches Jupiter early in the month, passes it on Nov. 16, then spends the rest of the month sailing away to the east.

articles.title: 9 nightmarish sci-fi spaceships to crawl aboard for Halloween if you dare
articles.excerpt: Grab your high-lumen flashlight and gargantuan gun to explore these vicious vessels
articles.body: Abandoned, possessed, or infested spaceships in sci-fi films, books, and video games are usually not a welcoming place to hang your helmet and kick back inside. Many are distinctly marked as DO NOT APPROACH zones and equipped with clearly articulated warning messages to keep your distance, but that doesn't ever seem to stop scavengers, space pirates, or evil industrial mega corporations from waving off these dangerous signs to board anyway. Other creaky craft are apt to contain nasty alien hitchhikers or biological hazards not exactly conducive to a pleasant star-trekking voyage. Whether these nefarious neglected craft have just reappeared from the other side of a black hole or have been lying dormant for eons on a hostile planetoid, visitors are usually infrequent.

articles.title: Anthropic VS code extension on Cursor backdoored for nearly 12 hours
articles.excerpt: It's still unknown how attackers got access to Anthropic's verified Cursor account.
articles.body: An official extension for Anthropic’s Claude model was backdoored and threatened as many as 5,000 developers' machines, multiple sources reported Friday. Anthropic so far has yet to warn customers of the incident. The compromised package was a VS Code extension available in the marketplace of Cursor, a maker of AI-assisted developer tools, the company said Friday. The malicious version, 2.1.313, subsequently affected “at most 5,000 users,” presumably when they either downloaded it or their systems automatically fetched and installed it. Anthropic pushed version 2.1.314 several hours after the previous version became available on Cursor, according to independent researcher Kevin Beaumont.
